canal-h2.title: 大运河
trans: China is large, and the north and south are far apart.
The north is cold and the south is hot.
A great deal of rice can be grown in the southern fields.
But getting that rice to the north was very inconvenient.
It took many days on foot, and the road was not safe.
The Sui emperor thought of a great plan.
He decided to dig a very, very long canal.
This canal ran all the way from the south to the north.
Many people came to dig it, and the digging went on for many years.
The work was hard and tiring, and some never went home again.
But once it was finished, north and south were much closer.
Merchants could go by boat and send goods far away.
Because a boat is faster than walking, goods became cheaper too.
Towns slowly grew up along both banks of the canal.
Fourteen hundred years have passed, and people still use the Grand Canal today.

canal2-h2.title: 坐船游玩
trans: Last month, Mum and Dad took me out on a boat.
We got up at six in the morning.
Because it was a long drive to the river, we had to set out early.
At the river I saw many boats.
Ours was not large, but it was very clean.
When the boat set off, I was a little scared.
But the boat moved slowly and gently on the water, and I soon stopped being afraid.
A breeze came across, and it was not hot at all.
I saw many fish in the water, swimming to and fro.
A few birds in the sky followed our boat the whole way.
At noon, Mum took out the food she had made that morning.
We ate and looked at the hills on either side.
Dad said that long ago there were many boats carrying rice on this river.
At three in the afternoon, the boat came back to the bank.
The day went by fast, and I remember it still.

dongzhou2-h2.title: 猫和老鼠
trans: Once there was a cat and a mouse, living in the same big house.
The house was big, with plenty to eat inside.
Every day the cat wanted to eat the mouse, but the mouse ran so fast that it had never once caught it.
One morning, the cat thought of a plan.
It hid behind the door, perfectly still, and waited for the mouse to come out.
The moment the mouse came out, the cat sprang.
The mouse got a fright and ran outside at once.
It ran across the fields, across the river, all the way up the mountain.
The mountain path was too long; the cat could run no further and sat at the foot of the mountain panting.
It looked up at the mountain and could not say a word.
The mouse reached the top and found water, flowers, and lots of good things to eat.
Best of all, there was no cat there.
So the mouse decided to live on the mountain and not go down again.
The cat waited at the foot of the mountain for a long time, and in the end had no choice but to go home alone.
From then on, the mouse lived safe and happy on the mountain.

han-h2.title: 丝绸之路
trans: In the Han dynasty, Chinese people did not know what lay to the west.
The emperor wanted to know how things were in the west, so he sent a man called Zhang Qian to take a look.
Zhang Qian travelled for many years before he came back, and met many hardships on the way.
When he returned he said: "There are many countries in the west, with fine horses and many new things."
When Chinese merchants heard this, they wanted to go west to trade too.
They carried silk, because people in the west loved silk.
Silk is light and beautiful, and can be carried a long way.
The road was long, over high mountains and through hot deserts, and very hard going.
One round trip often took a year or two.
Merchants from the west came too, bringing fine horses and grapes.
Not only goods, but ideas and knowledge passed back and forth along this road too.
Because the most famous thing on the road was silk, people later called it the Silk Road.
This road joined China to places very far away.
Zhang Qian was the first to travel this road.
So people say it was he who opened the door between China and the West.

han2-h2.title: 我的小猫
trans: We have a little cat at home; its name is Little White.
It came to us last year, when it was still very small.
It is white all over, and only its eyes are black.
Every morning it wakes me up.
If I do not get up, it sits on my head and watches me.
After I get up, the first thing I do is feed it.
It likes fish best, and does not eat much else.
After eating, it plays with a ball for a while.
Sometimes it jumps onto my books and goes to sleep, and then I cannot read.
When I leave for school, it watches me from the doorway.
When I come home in the afternoon, it runs over and gives a little cry.
Although it cannot talk, I know it is glad.
At night it sleeps by my bed, without stirring.
Once it fell ill; I was very worried and took it to the vet.
I love my little cat; it is my best friend.

konfucius-h2.title: 孔子的学生

sents.mn: to go to school; to study

trans: More than two thousand five hundred years ago, there was a teacher in China whose name was Confucius.
In those days, only the children of wealthy families could go to school.
Confucius said: "Whoever wants to learn, I will teach."
So his students grew more and more numerous, grown-ups and young people alike.
They read with Confucius, discussed with him, and travelled with him to learn.
Confucius often said: "After you learn something, think it over often; only then do you truly learn it."
He also said: "If you do not know a thing, simply ask; do not be afraid to ask."
A student asked him: "What is a good person?"
He said: "What you do not want yourself, do not give to others."
He also said: "Be good to your parents and good to your friends; that is a good person."
Although he long wanted to serve as an official and work for the state, he did not succeed.
So he put all his time into teaching his students.
After he died, his students wrote down what he had said, in a book called the Analects.
Because of this book, we still know his thinking today.
More than two thousand years have passed, and Chinese people still remember Confucius's words.

ming-h2.title: 郑和下西洋

sents.mn: Zheng He, admiral of the treasure fleet
Zheng He, admiral of the treasure fleet
to know; to become aware of

trans: More than six hundred years ago the Ming had a great fleet.
The man who led it was called Zheng He.
His ships were enormous, bigger than many houses.
One ship could hold several hundred people.
On board were water, rice and many other things.
They carried Chinese silk, tea and beautiful goods.
The fleet set out from China and sailed west.
They crossed a great sea.
Some places were very hot, some very far.
They met many different peoples.
They did not go to make war on those countries.
They only traded, and then came back.
People of other lands gave them animals they had never seen.
Zheng He made the voyage seven times in all.
So in those days many countries knew of China.

ming2-h2.title: 奇妙的发现

sents.mn: to like; to be fond of
to know; to become aware of
to look; to watch; to read
to like; to be fond of
to like; to be fond of
to look; to watch; to read
to look; to watch; to read
to look; to watch; to read

trans: Two men of the Ming spent their lives looking for answers.
The first loved the plants and trees of the hills.
He wanted to know which of them could be medicine.
Because the old books had a great deal that was wrong.
So he decided to go and see for himself.
He walked a great deal and asked a great many people.
He also tried some of the plants himself.
He spent nearly thirty years and wrote a great book.
In it were more than a thousand kinds of plant and medicine.
The second loved walking, and looking at mountains and rivers.
He went to many places no one else had been.
Some paths were hard going, but he did not turn back.
Every evening he wrote down what he had seen that day.
He wrote for decades, filling many volumes.
Both men did the same thing: go and see for themselves, then write it down.

paper-h2.title: 纸的故事
trans: Long ago, China had no paper yet.
People wrote characters on bamboo, and one book took a great deal of bamboo.
Bamboo was heavy and bulky, and one person could not carry it.
If you wanted to send a friend a book, it was a hard thing to do.
The wealthy also wrote on silk, but silk was too expensive.
In the Eastern Han, there was a man called Cai Lun.
He thought: "Could we make something light and cheap to write on?"
He put tree bark, old cloth and torn fishing nets in water, and pounded them into small pieces.
Then he made them into a thin sheet, and once it had dried in the sun, it was paper.
Paper was light and cheap, and easy to write on.
With paper, students could carry books to school, and teachers could write out the lesson for everyone to read.
Because paper was so useful, it slowly spread to other countries.
Today, people all over the world use paper.
And it began in China.
Cai Lun's invention changed China, and changed the world.

paper2-h2.title: 书里的世界
trans: My favourite thing is books.
My room is full of books, all over the place.
Some are new, and some are already very old.
Books are full of interesting stories.
Some books tell of things long ago: emperors, the Great Wall, and Dayu.
Some books tell of the birds in the sky and the fish in the water.
When I read, it is as if I have gone somewhere far away.
Sometimes I read so intently that I do not even hear Mum calling me.
Mum says: "Reading lets you know many things, and makes you a better person."
She also says I can ask her about any character I do not know.
So I often keep a small notebook with me.
When I meet a new character, I write it down.
Every evening I read for a while.
Although I have already read many books, I want to read more.
The world inside books is far bigger than our room.

print-h2.title: 印书的故事
trans: Once there was paper, people could write books.
But books then were written out one character at a time.
Writing one book took many days, sometimes months.
So books were few and expensive, and only the very wealthy could afford them.
Later, someone thought of a good way.
They carved the characters into a wooden board.
Once carved, they brushed ink onto the board.
Then they laid paper on it and pressed with the hand.
When it was lifted, the characters were on the paper.
Because one board could be used many times, printing was very fast.
A day could print what once took a month to write.
Once books were cheap, more people read.
Not only the rich, but ordinary people too could read.
Later, people of the Song carved the characters one by one on small wooden blocks, which could be swapped after printing.
This method spread to other countries and changed the world.

print2-h2.title: 图书馆的一天
trans: This afternoon, the teacher took us to the library.
The library is big and tall, and the books go from the floor right up to the top.
The moment we went in, everyone stopped talking, because many people inside were reading.
Some books were new, and some already old.
The teacher said: "You may look for a book you want to read yourselves."
I walked around for a long time and at last found a book of stories from ancient times.
In it were emperors, the Great Wall, and a very long road.
I sat down, and once I started reading I read for two hours.
I read so intently that I forgot the time.
Only when the teacher called me did I get up.
I took three books home.
Mum said: "So many, can you finish them?"
I said: "I certainly can!"
That night I read until very late before I slept.
Two weeks later, I had finished all three books.

qin-h2.title: 万里长城
trans: More than two thousand years ago, China had many small states.
These states were always at war, for hundreds of years, and life was hard for everyone.
Later, Qin Shi Huang defeated the other states one by one and made China one country.
He was China's first emperor.
He did a great deal: he made everyone in the country write the same characters and use the same money.
He also made the roads the same width and the carts the same size across the country.
This way, people across the country could travel and trade with one another.
But riders from the north often came to attack China.
Qin Shi Huang decided to build a very, very long wall in the north.
Many people came to do this work, and it went on for many years.
They laid earth and stone in place piece by piece.
Although the work was tiring and hard, the wall grew longer year by year.
The wall runs along the mountains, on to where it can no longer be seen.
Because it is so long, people call it the Ten-Thousand-Li Great Wall.
More than two thousand years have passed, and today we can still go and see it.

qin2-h2.title: 爬山的孩子
trans: Last Saturday, the teacher took us to climb the mountain.
The morning weather was fine, and not hot at all.
We met at the school gate at eight; twenty of us went in all.
The mountain path was long, with trees on both sides and birds singing in them.
We walked, talked and looked at the scenery all at once.
After an hour of walking, I began to feel tired.
I sat under a tree, drank some water, and said: "I don't want to go on."
A friend came over and said: "Almost there, keep going!"
He added: "If we go back now, we won't see the view from the top."
I thought about it, stood up, and followed the others on.
We walked another half hour, and at last reached the top.
Looking down from the top, the school was as small as a dot and the road was like a line.
We shouted: "We did it!"
On the way down, I did not feel tired at all any more.
Although it was tiring, I was glad I had not given up.

qing-h2.title: 康熙皇帝

sents.mn: to like; to be fond of
(measure word for flat things); to open
although; even though (often used correlatively with 是 or 是 etc)

trans: The Qing dynasty had a famous emperor called Kangxi.
He became emperor at the age of eight.
Because he was so young, others helped him at first.
Only in his teens did he begin to rule himself.
He was emperor for sixty-one years in all.
He rose very early every day to work.
He loved learning new things.
He studied mathematics, and learning that came from the west.
People from the west told him about the heavens.
He also had many books made for him.
He sent men across the whole country to make a great map.
At that time China was far larger than before.
He cared about the farmers, and asked about many places.
Although being emperor was exhausting, he never stopped.
So many say he was one of China’s finest emperors.

qing2-h2.title: 故宫里的秘密

sents.mn: outside (also pr. [wài mian] for this sense)
to look; to watch; to read
to look; to watch; to read

trans: In Beijing there is a very large, very old place called the Forbidden City.
It was built for a Ming emperor more than six hundred years ago.
Building it took more than ten years.
Inside are more than nine thousand rooms.
If you slept in one room a night, it would take over twenty years.
The outer gates are high and great.
The buildings are red, and very beautiful.
The emperor worked in the largest hall.
Every morning many officials came to see him.
As they came in they dared not say a word more than needed.
Because there was so much here that had to be done just so.
Many beautiful things were kept inside.
There is writing, there are books, and things made of gold.
In the past ordinary people could not go in.
But today anyone may go in and look.

reform-h2.title: 改变的时代

sents.mn: although; even though (often used correlatively with 是 or 是 etc)

trans: As the Qing dynasty neared its end, China faced many difficulties.
By then countries in the west had built new ships.
Their ships were large and fast, and could move without wind.
They had new things that China did not.
Because of this, China went through several very hard decades.
Many began to ask: what should we do?
Some said we must learn the west’s knowledge.
So some officials began founding new schools.
Those schools taught mathematics, and other countries' languages.
They also sent young people abroad to study.
Those young people did a great deal after they returned.
Some built ships, some built roads.
Doing all this was far from easy.
Although they failed many times, they did not give up.
Their thinking shaped the China that came after.

reform2-h2.title: 变化中的上海

sents.mn: to think that ...; to feel that ...
to think that ...; to feel that ...
(joins a verb to how it is done)

trans: A hundred years ago and more, Shanghai was still only a small place.
Few people lived there then.
Because it lies by the sea, many ships later came.
People from many countries settled there.
They brought new things and new ideas.
The city gained new schools.
And newspapers that came out every day.
Cars appeared in the streets, and many shops.
At night the streets were bright, with people out until late.
The old China and the new things were both in this city.
Some thought it good, some did not.
Some traded here and made a great deal of money.
And many others lived very hard lives.
So Shanghai was a place both new and hard.
Its change was China’s change in those years.

republic-h2.title: 新中国的梦
republic-h2.en: The Dream of a New China

sents.mn: to look; to watch; to read
although; even though (often used correlatively with 是 or 是 etc)

trans: A little over a hundred years ago China still had an emperor.
But life in those days was very hard.
Many thought: China must be different.
There was a man called Sun Yat-sen.
When he was young he studied how to treat the sick.
He had been to many countries and seen a great deal.
He found that other countries did well without an emperor.
So he said: the country belongs to everyone.
He believed the Chinese people could do it themselves.
Many young people worked with him.
They tried many times without success.
But he never gave up.
In 1912 the new state began.
The new government built new schools and new roads.
Although the road ahead was still hard, people had hope.

republic2-h2.title: 新时代的年轻人
republic2-h2.en: Young People of a New Age

sents.mn: outside (also pr. [wài mian] for this sense)
(joins a verb to how it is done)

trans: A hundred years ago China had many young people.
They were very different from those before them.
They attended the new schools.
The schools taught mathematics, and western learning.
Some even went abroad to study.
They lived overseas for some years.
Because they saw so much that was new, they thought more deeply.
After finishing, many came back.
Some became teachers, some doctors.
Their way of doing things was not the old way.
They wrote new books, in language everyone could understand.
Because of this, more and more people could read.
They made new things and asked new questions.
They wanted to make their country better.
They said: study can change a country.

rider-h2.title: 草原骑手
trans: Far to the north of China lies a vast grassland.
There are no mountains there, only sky and grass.
In winter life was very hard, with strong winds and heavy snow.
Long ago, a people lived there called the Khitan.
They had to follow the water and the grass and move house often, so they lived in tents.
A tent could be folded up and carried away, and opened again in a new place.
They learned to ride from childhood, and grown-ups and children alike rode fast and well.
Their horses were fast and fine too.
They wanted to write their own language down, so later they made a writing of their own.
They traded with the Song in the south.
They sold horses and bought tea, cloth and other things.
Although the two sides sometimes fought, trade never stopped.
So the things of north and south grew more and more alike.
They lived in the north for more than two hundred years.
Today there are still people on the grassland living in tents, riding and grazing their cattle and horses.

rider2-h2.title: 草原上的风
trans: The wind on the grassland blows all year round.
When it comes, all the grass moves.
From far off it looks like water.
Children who live here learn to ride very young.
By three or four they have a horse of their own.
They ride fast, and are not afraid at all.
In the morning they go out with the grown-ups to graze the cattle and horses.
They watch the cattle and horses grazing, all day long.
At midday they eat outside, and only come back in the evening.
The night is dark, but the stars above are very bright.
Because a city has so many lights, you cannot see stars like these in a city.
They sing outside, and the singing carries far.
Winter is cold and summer windy; life on the grassland is not easy.
But they love it here.
They say: "This is our place."

sanguo-h2.title: 诸葛亮的智慧
trans: After the Han, China split into three states, called the Three Kingdoms.
The three states were always at war.
At that time there was a very clever man called Zhuge Liang.
When he was young he lived in the hills and read every day.
Liu Bei went to ask him three times before he came out to help.
Because he knew so much, everyone listened to him.
He could read the weather, and he was very good at finding a way.
Once, the enemy came, but there were very few soldiers in the city.
Everyone was anxious.
Zhuge Liang did not close the city gate; instead he sat alone on the wall playing the qin.
When the enemy arrived and saw the gate open, they thought it very strange.
They thought: "There must be many soldiers inside; going in is too dangerous."
So they did not dare go in, and left.
Zhuge Liang did a great deal for his state all his life, until he was very old.
To this day, people still tell his story.

sanguo2-h2.title: 好朋友的力量
trans: I have three very good friends.
We are at the same school and in the same class.
Every day at noon, the four of us eat together.
After class we often play together too.
Sometimes we do not think the same way, but after talking it over it is soon fine.
Last month I fell ill and could not go to school.
I was at home alone and felt very bored.
On the third day, the three of them came to see me.
They brought fruit, and two books.
They sat by my bed and told me what was happening at school.
One told stories, two laughed, and I laughed along too.
Hearing it made me happy, and I forgot at once that I was ill.
As they left they said: "Get well soon, we are waiting for you."
By the next morning I already felt much better.
I think good friends really can make a person well.

scholar-h2.title: 勤学的年轻人
trans: In the Jin dynasty, many different peoples lived in the north.
They spoke differently and wrote differently.
Because everyone had to live and trade together, many young people began to learn Chinese characters.
They went to school very early every day.
The teacher taught them to read first, and only then to write.
One character had to be written many times over.
If it was not good, they wrote it once more.
Some were still reading in the evening.
Because there was no lamp at home, they sat by the door to read.
Once they had learned the characters, they could find good work.
Some became officials, some merchants, and some teachers.
They did not forget their own writing either, and knew both scripts.
They read the books of both sides together, and knew more than others.
They said: "A person who has studied well can get on anywhere."
We learn Chinese characters today for the same reason.

scholar2-h2.title: 学者的笔记
trans: In the Jin dynasty there was a man who loved to read.
His family had no money, but it had many books.
Every morning he read as soon as he got up.
He read every kind of book: history, poetry, and books on herbal medicine.
He had a notebook, and always kept it on him.
Whenever he read a good sentence, he copied it down at once.
He wrote his own thoughts underneath.
Year after year, the notebooks grew.
He kept them all in a large chest.
Later he grew old, his eyes were poor, and he could write no more.
He gave the chest to his students.
The students put what was in the notebooks in order and made a book.
Many years later people were still reading the book, because in it was all the knowledge he had gathered in his life.
So it is said that his book has gone on teaching.
He himself had said: "If you do not write it down, you soon forget."

shang-h2.title: 骨头上的字
trans: The Shang was one of China's very early dynasties, more than three thousand years ago.
People of that time could already write.
But they did not write on paper, because there was no paper yet.
They carved the characters on animal bones.
These bones were big and white, and many characters could be carved on them.
The Shang people believed there were gods in the sky.
So when they had a question, they asked the gods.
They asked: "Will the weather be good today?"
They also asked: "If we go to war this time, will we win?"
After asking, they burned the bone with fire.
Cracks would appear on the bone, and they read the cracks to find the answer.
Then they carved both the question and the answer on that bone.
These are China's earliest characters, more than three thousand years old.
Long afterwards, people discovered these bones in the ground.
So today we can still see the characters the Shang people carved.

shang2-h2.title: 市场的一天
trans: Every Saturday is market day.
At seven in the morning, Mum and I go to the market together.
There are already many people at the market, and it is very lively.
Some people sell fruit, some sell fish, and some sell vegetables and meat.
The fruit seller calls out: "Sweet apples, three yuan each!"
I buy three apples and eat one first; it really is sweet.
Mum buys a fish, some vegetables, and a lot of fruit.
She says: "Tonight Grandma is coming to our house for dinner."
There is too much to carry, so I carry two bags for Mum.
On the way home, we see many people carrying vegetables too.
When we get home, Mum starts cooking and I help her wash the vegetables.
In the evening Grandma comes, and the whole family eats together.
Grandma says: "This fish is cooked so well!"
Mum smiles and says: "I bought it this morning, it's very fresh."
Market day is my favourite day.

shufa-h2.title: 写字高手
trans: Chinese people have long felt that writing is a beautiful thing.
More than sixteen hundred years ago, in the Jin dynasty, there was a very famous man.
His name was Wang Xizhi.
He began learning to write when he was very small.
He practised every day and never stopped for a single day.
After writing, he went to the river to wash his brush.
Because he washed it for so many years, the water in the river turned black.
The characters he wrote were beautiful; some were like wind, some like water.
So people called him the "Sage of Calligraphy".
One spring, he met many friends in the mountains.
The weather that day was fine, and they drank wine and wrote poems.
He put everyone's poems together and wrote a passage at the front.
That piece became the most famous calligraphy in China.
More than a thousand years have passed, and many people still study his calligraphy.
People say that to learn calligraphy you must do as he did: practise every day, and never stop.

shufa2-h2.title: 学写汉字
trans: This month, we started learning to write Chinese characters.
First the teacher taught us how to hold the pen.
She said: "Sit up straight, and only then will your characters look good."
She also said not to write too fast.
We started with the two characters 水 and 山.
These two look easy, but writing them well is not.
Because a character has many strokes, which one to write first matters.
I wrote one character more than thirty times, and it still was not good.
The teacher looked and said: "Don't rush, write slowly."
I wrote slowly, and day by day I wrote better and better.
A month later, the teacher said: "Much better than last month."
I showed Mum my best character.
She said it was lovely, and put it up in her room.
Now I want to write a little every day.
I feel every Chinese character is interesting.

song-h2.title: 中国的四大发明
trans: Chinese people made many useful inventions, and four of them are the most famous.
The first is paper.
It was paper that let people write books, and let knowledge travel further.
The second is printing.
Song people carved the characters one by one on small wooden blocks that could be swapped after printing; this is called movable-type printing.
With printing, books became plentiful and cheap.
The third is the compass.
It is small, but its needle always points south.
Far from home at sea, a ship with a compass did not lose its way.
The fourth is gunpowder.
At first people used it only for fireworks; at festivals the sky was red and bright.
Later it came to be used for other things too.
These four inventions slowly spread to other countries.
They let people read, sail the seas and celebrate, and changed the way wars were fought.
So it is said that these four inventions changed the whole world.

song2-h2.title: 纸币的故事
trans: Long ago, people bought things with money made of gold and copper.
This money was small, but heavy.
If you were buying only a little, it was fine.
But a merchant bought a great deal at once, so he had to carry a great deal of money.
The money was too heavy for one person to carry; it had to be pulled in a cart.
And the road was not safe: there were people who made a living robbing merchants.
Song people thought of a way.
A merchant left his money at one particular shop, and the shop gave him a paper receipt.
On the receipt was written how much it was worth, and the shop's name.
The receipt was made of paper, light and small, easy to carry on you.
In another city, that receipt could be exchanged for the money.
This was the earliest paper money in the world.
With paper money, merchants could travel further, and trade in the cities grew and grew.
Later, other countries began to use paper money too.
Today many countries still use paper money.

tang-h2.title: 长安的繁华
trans: More than thirteen hundred years ago, China had a great dynasty called the Tang.
The Tang's biggest city was Chang'an.
At that time it was the biggest city in the world, with more than a million people living in it.
Its streets were straight and long, and took a long time to walk.
Because the Tang was so famous, people came from many countries.
Some came to trade, some to study, and some just to see the great city.
They brought horses, fruit, and new instruments and music.
So people in the city could eat food from far away, and hear music from far away.
The Tang also had many famous poets.
The most famous of them was called Li Bai.
He wrote many beautiful poems, which people still read today.
In those days women could study, and could ride horses.
At night the city was bright with lights, and people sang and danced in the streets.
Although Chang'an later grew smaller, its story remained.
Many say the Tang was one of China's finest times.

tang2-h2.title: 诗人看月亮
trans: The Tang dynasty had a very famous poet called Li Bai.
He travelled to many places in his life.
Because he was so often away, he seldom went home.
What he loved most was the moon.
One night he was staying away from home, alone.
The weather that night was fine, without a breath of wind.
When he got up, he saw the ground was all white.
At first he thought there was frost on the ground.
Only then did he realise it was moonlight.
He looked up at the moon and thought of his home far away.
He thought of his mother, and of old friends.
His heart felt a little sad.
So he sat down and wrote a very short poem.
The poem has only four lines, but every Chinese person knows it by heart.
Because people away from home think of home too when they look at the moon.

tao-h2.title: 田里的诗人
trans: More than sixteen hundred years ago, in the Jin dynasty, there was a famous poet called Tao Yuanming.
When he was young he served as an official.
An official could have money, and could have a name.
But he did not like that life at all.
Because an official has to say things he does not want to say every day, and do things he does not want to do.
So one day, he decided to stop.
He went back to his own home and began to farm.
He grew rice and vegetables, and planted many flowers as well.
In the morning he worked in the fields; in the evening he wrote poems.
His poems were not long, but very beautiful.
In his poems he said that in the fields his heart was free.
Although his family was not rich, he lived happily.
Someone asked him: "Looking back, do you think it was the right choice?"
He said: "I do not want much; this is enough."
More than a thousand years have passed, and Chinese people still read his poems.

tao2-h2.title: 下雨天
trans: This morning, the moment I got up I saw the sky was dark.
A little later, it began to rain.
The rain grew heavier and heavier, so I could not go out to play.
I sat by the window and watched the rain outside.
The rain hit the ground with a lovely sound.
People in the street were walking fast; a child ran past, soaked through.
At first I felt a little bored.
Then I decided to read at home.
Mum made me a cup of hot tea.
She took a book too, and sat down beside me.
Neither of us spoke, and the room was very quiet.
By the afternoon the rain slowly eased.
The sky brightened a little, and outside looked very clean.
The leaves were covered in water, and when the sun came out they shone.
I think a rainy day has its good side too.

tea-h2.title: 一杯好茶
trans: Chinese people began drinking tea very early.
By the Song dynasty, tea was already an everyday thing.
Tea is made from the leaves of the tea tree.
In spring, people pick the newly grown leaves.
Then the leaves are dried in the sun and roasted over and over before they can be drunk.
Before drinking tea, the water must first be boiled.
The water must be neither too hot nor too cold.
With the wrong water, even good tea leaves make a poor cup.
Song people took their tea seriously.
They looked at the tea's colour first, then smelled it, and only then drank slowly.
They felt that drinking tea was not only about quenching thirst.
Over tea, a person can grow quiet and think things over slowly.
So many people talked with friends over tea.
Later, tea spread from China to many countries around the world.
To this day, Chinese people still love drinking tea.

tea2-h2.title: 茶馆的故事
trans: Song cities had many teahouses.
A teahouse opened early, because many people came in the morning.
Some came to drink tea, some came to meet friends.
Merchants talked business here, discussing over tea what to buy and sell.
Old people talked here about times long past.
Children came too, and sat at the back listening.
In the afternoon, a storyteller would come.
He told them so well that everyone listened, rapt.
In the stories were emperors, generals, and dragons.
At the most gripping moment he would stop and say: "More tomorrow."
One story took several days, so everyone came back the next day.
The teahouse was also where you heard the news.
Whatever was new in the city, the people in the teahouse knew first.
So it is said that the teahouse is a city's ears.
In China today you can still find teahouses like that.

xia-h2.title: 大禹治水
trans: Long, long ago, it rained in China for many days, and a great flood came.
The flood went into the fields, and into many people's homes.
People had nowhere to live, and could only go up the mountains to live.
The king of that time was anxious, and asked everyone: "Who can control the flood?"
Someone said: "Dayu is a good man, and good at finding a way. Let him come."
After Dayu came, he did not start work at once; he first went to see where the water came from and where it went.
He found that if you only blocked the water with earth, it would come back.
So he decided to open a road for the water, and let it flow out to the sea.
He led many people in digging channels, and the digging went on for thirteen years.
Although he missed home very much, he never went back.
Three times he walked to his own door, and did not go in.
Later the water went down, and people returned to farm the fields.
Everyone was grateful to Dayu, and the king passed the throne to him.
To this day, Chinese people still tell the story of Dayu controlling the flood.
People say that when you meet a problem, you should do as Dayu did: think of a way first, then start work.

xia2-h2.title: 小龙学游泳
trans: Many little dragons lived in the river, and they played in the water every day.
Among them was one little dragon who still could not swim.
Every morning it sat on the bank and watched the other dragons playing in the water.
The river was deep and cold, and it dared not go in.
It thought: "What if I fall in?"
Its mother saw, and said to it: "Don't be afraid, you can learn it. I will teach you."
Mother swam first to show it, and then let it get into the water slowly.
The little dragon got in, and at first swallowed several mouthfuls of water.
It tried once, twice, three times, and still had not learned.
It felt a little like giving up, but its mother said: "Try once more."
The little dragon did not give up, and came to the river every day to practise.
A month later, it finally learned to swim.
It swam better and better, faster than all the other little dragons.
Now the little dragon plays in the water with its friends every day, very happy.
It says: "What you cannot do, practise a lot, and then you can."

yuan-h2.title: 马可·波罗来华
trans: More than seven hundred years ago, China had a great dynasty called the Yuan.
The Yuan emperor was Kublai Khan.
His realm was vast, reaching from the east far into the west.
Because the roads were safer than before, more people travelled.
In those days a young man set out from Italy; his name was Marco Polo.
He travelled with his father and uncle, and it took more than three years to reach China.
They crossed high mountains and hot deserts.
After reaching China, he lived in Dadu for seventeen years.
Kublai liked him, and sent him to see many places.
He saw many cities and many people.
He said China's cities were far bigger than those of his own country.
He was struck too that people here used paper money, and burned a kind of black stone for warmth in winter.
After going home, he told others what he had seen, and someone wrote it into a book.
Many people did not believe the book, because what it told was too strange.
But because of this book, Europeans learned of the world to the east for the first time.

yuan2-h2.title: 元朝的美食
trans: In the Yuan dynasty, people came to China from many places.
So there were many more kinds of food in China.
People from the north ate lamb from childhood.
They also drank milk tea, which is tea boiled with milk, white and hot.
A cup of it in cold weather warmed a person up at once.
Merchants from the west brought new spices.
Some spices went into meat, some into soup, and they smelled wonderful.
Once the spices were added, the meat tasted quite different.
People in the south still preferred rice and fish.
People from the west liked bread, and liked grapes.
So one country had many kinds of good food.
In a big city you could eat food from far away.
Marco Polo wrote down the food he had eaten too.
He said his own country had nothing like some of it.
So food, too, is one way people of different places come to know one another.

zhou-h2.title: 天命的故事
trans: After the Shang, China had a new dynasty called the Western Zhou.
The Western Zhou king wanted everyone to obey him.
So he said something that became very famous.
He said: "It is Heaven that made me king."
He also said that Heaven is always watching every king.
If a king does well, Heaven lets him go on.
If a king does badly, Heaven gives the throne to someone else.
So a king cannot think only of himself.
He must care for the people, for the farmers and for the soldiers.
In those days, many people farmed the fields.
The weather was good, and the crops in the fields grew well.
There was rice at home, and meat too, and life was not bad.
The king made many new rules, and everyone had to follow them.
Although the Western Zhou later ended, this idea remained.
To this day, Chinese people still speak of the "Mandate of Heaven".

zhou2-h2.title: 大树下的朋友
trans: There is a very big tree at our school gate.
The teacher says the tree is older than the school; it is more than a hundred years old.
In spring the tree is covered in blossom; in summer it is cool underneath.
My friends and I play under the big tree every day.
When the weather is nice, we sit under the tree and read.
We play games, tell stories, and race to see who runs fastest.
My best friend is Xiaoming, and he can tell many lovely stories.
Today he told the story of Dayu controlling the flood, and told it very well.
We listened so intently that we did not hear the bell for class.
The teacher came over and said with a smile: "Time for class!"
We all said: "Goodbye, big tree!" and ran into the classroom.
After class, we ran back to the tree.
In autumn the leaves turn yellow and fall one by one.
We pick the leaves up and make them into bookmarks.
This big tree is our best friend.
